notes.text: I'm going to begin by reading through the mission briefing.

I'm laying out the six unknowns: the test drops should reveal impact, fall time, whether the load went into the smoke, and the wind at aircraft altitude. Each drop samples wind at its own height, so varying the release altitudes would expose shear and veer, while fall time tells me about drag and any updraft inside the smoke.

I'm weighing a first test drop at 100 m, heading 90 at 60 m/s, placed at x=-200 and y=0, away from the fire so the smoke column doesn't skew the result. I'm noting the updraft inside the smoke is still an open unknown that later drops might reveal.

I'm working out the wind at 100 m, which blows roughly east at 6.7. The observed fall time of 7.81 s is well above the 4.52 s a drag-free drop would take, so drag is clearly a factor. I'm now tracking the horizontal displacement and the aircraft's eastward motion against the wind to get the relative velocity to the air.

I'm weighing the drag estimate against the observed fall time, which suggests drag around 0.03 to 0.05. Next I'll run a drop at 40 m altitude to see how the wind shear changes things.

I'm settling on a second test drop at 150 m, heading due north from x=-200, y=-300, so it stays well clear of the fire and its smoke column.

I'm checking the wind figures at 150 m and 100 m: 7.9 m/s and 6.7 m/s, which gives a shear exponent of about 0.41. With 0.5 m/s noise that estimate is shaky, and the veer of roughly 4° per 100 m is about the size of the noise, so it could be small.

I'm recomputing the second drop's horizontal and vertical displacement, which gives about 62 m north and 68 m east over a fall of roughly 10.9 s, longer than the 7.8 s a no-drag fall from 150 m would take. Next I'll run a comparison with a candidate drag coefficient and wind profile to see how far the predictions miss both drops.

I'm working out the horizontal motion now: the load's velocity relative to the air decays fast under drag, so most of the early displacement isn't just wind drift. That relaxation distance is what should account for the gap between the roughly 55 m I'd expect from wind alone and the 107 m observed.

I'm estimating how far the load drifts horizontally under drag: with the drag coefficient around 0.04 and the initial relative speed near 53 m/s, the logarithmic relaxation distance over the fall comes to roughly 70 m relative to the air, which together with the wind drift lands in the neighborhood of the observed 107 m. Next I want to work out which parts of the data pin down drag, wind, shear, and veer, and whether the smoke entries can reveal an updraft.

I'm weighing how an updraft might show up in the data: drops that pass through the smoke column above the fire should reveal it, and a test drop over the fire center at moderate altitude would help pin that down. The targets sit far from the calibration fire and have their own intensities and smoke columns, so a load that clips a target's plume could be pushed off course, which matters since the score drops quickly beyond a few meters.

I'm checking the fall-time residuals, which show the predicted times running 0.15 and 0.29 seconds longer than observed. That would mean the model needs a bit more drag, but I'm second-guessing the direction, since more drag should lengthen the fall, and I catch that dt is predicted minus observed, so a positive value means the prediction is too long.

I need to lower the drag, since higher drag would lengthen the predicted fall. That should also shift the drop 2 vertical residual, because less drag keeps more of the northward velocity. I'll try a drag value of 0.035.

I've got the drag estimate narrowed to about 0.0375 from the two drop interpolations, and now I'm moving on to the dx/dy residuals.

I'm working through the dx and dy residuals at the 0.0375 drag estimate, and the second drop's dy of about -2.8 suggests a northward wind component or a different wind speed than I assumed. Since impact noise is around 1.5 m, these residuals are a bit ambiguous. I'm planning a few more test drops: one at low altitude to pin down the shear, one on a different heading to check the veer, and one through the smoke to look for an updraft.

I'm weighing a test drop released right over the smoke column at altitude 100, heading west at 45 m/s, to see whether the updraft lengthens the fall. The wind drift and the updraft scaling near the ground both matter for how the load falls through that region, so I'd rather check the path in a simulation than guess.

I'm checking whether a drop released right over the fire at altitude 100, heading east at 45 m/s, would tell me the updraft strength, since the load should leave the smoke quickly but spend some time inside it. Inside the smoke the updraft should be strongest at the center and weaken toward the edge, so the fall time difference would reveal it once drag is known.

I'm settling on a test drop directly over the fire at altitude 100, heading 90 at 60 m/s, so I can compare its fall time with drop 1 and read off the updraft. Inside the 50 m smoke radius the horizontal drift should keep the load there for a few seconds, and if the updraft is around 10 that could add a second or two to the fall, which should be detectable.

I'm checking whether a drop released right over the fire would land near 107 east of the release point, given the uniform wind. Inside the 50 m smoke radius the load would only spend about a second, so I'd rather use a slow, head-into-the-wind approach so the load lingers in the updraft.

I'm weighing a test drop released upwind of the fire, around x = -40 to -50, at a slower 45 m/s heading east, so the load drifts into the smoke column and the updraft's effect on the fall time becomes measurable.

I'm going to test the simulator with a drop from x=-50 heading east at 45 m/s, to see where it lands and whether it crosses the smoke. After that I want to check the wind direction at other altitudes, which the aircraft reports at its own height.

I'm settling on a low-altitude test drop at 40 m, heading 180 at 60 m/s from x=300, since the lower wind there should show the shear, and its distance from the fire keeps it from interfering.

I'm settling on a low-altitude test drop at 40 m, heading 180 at 60 m/s from x=300, since the wind near the ground should show the shear there and the distance from the fire keeps it clear of the smoke. I also want to account for the wind and heading noise, roughly 0.5 m/s and 4 degrees, when I compare the results.

I'm working out the wind shear exponent from the 40 m reading: 5.2 m/s at 94°, which against the 100 m value gives about 0.28, while the earlier 150 m pair gave 0.41, so I'm taking roughly 0.35 as an average. The measurements carry about 0.5 m/s of noise, which I need to keep in mind. Next I'm checking how the direction changes with height, 91° at 100 m, 93° at 150 m, and 94° at 40 m.

Veer looks close to zero on average, around a degree, so I'll treat it as small. Checking the drop 3 impact, the 15.8 m eastward offset and the 57.8 m southward drift over 3.96 s give a mean of about 14.6 m/s south, far below what the 60 m/s aircraft speed would suggest. That gap points to strong drag slowing the drop quickly. I'll now test a set of parameters, drag, wind speed, direction, shear, veer and updraft, against the residuals from all three drops.

The residuals on the x-axis are all negative, so the prediction is landing too far west. For drop 2 that's a -3.4 offset, which suggests the wind needs to push further east, or the wind speed needs to go up. The y-residual on drop 2 is -2.9, so I'm wondering whether the wind should also shift more northward, since that drop was heading north and the observed point sits farther north than predicted.

The wind direction of 92° points a touch south of due east, so a bit more northward component would help with the negative y-residual on drop 2. I'm estimating roughly 88° and a slight speed increase to close the eastward gap, though I'm still weighing that against the aircraft readings of 91–94° and 5–8 m/s.

I'm averaging the aircraft readings, which land around 6.7 m/s, and I'm also wondering whether drag could be behind the consistent eastward shortfall. My current guess is a wind direction near 89° with a speed of about 7.0 m/s.

The residuals are down to within about 1.5 m of noise, with the y-offsets sitting slightly high around +1 m. Next I need to account for updraft and wind veer, and I'm working through the veer using the direction measurements at three heights.

The veer looks small, probably within about ±10 degrees per 100 m, since the three direction readings barely differ once their 4° noise is taken into account. Next I'll turn to the updraft, which matters for targets sitting in smoke, and plan a test drop at the fire centre to see how strongly fall time depends on it.

I'm weighing a test drop from near the centre of the fire, with the aircraft heading west into the easterly wind so the load's relative speed is high at first and then drops off quickly. The idea is to find a release where the load lingers in the smoke for a while, so the fall time shows how strongly the updraft matters. I'll run a few candidate releases with an updraft of about 10 and see which one gives a useful impact and fall time.

With updraft 10 the fall time jumps to 15.31 from 7.76 without it, so the updraft is clearly a strong effect and a good signal to measure. Dropping from (0,0) heading 270 at speed 45 and altitude 100 should capture it well, even if the fall time gets long at higher updraft values.

I'm also weighing whether the lifted load, which sits higher and so falls longer, and the smoke column's drift could muddy the reading, but either way the test should still reveal the updraft value. So I'll go ahead and run it.

The updraft fall time of 9.4 is slower than the 7.76 predicted without one, so there is an updraft, and a weaker one. The impact point also shifted about 9 m east compared with the no-updraft prediction. I'll run the compare step with all four drops across a few updraft strengths, starting with 3 and 4.

I'm checking whether the dt residual of +0.11 at U=4 means I should lower U, using the slope of about 0.75 seconds per unit of U. That puts the estimate near 3.85, though the nonlinearity could shift it.

I'm weighing whether to try U=3.5 next, since the drag value from earlier could also be pulling the fall time, and the dx and dy residuals at U=4 are still unexplained.

Working the updraft estimate out from the two trial values, I land near U ≈ 3.8, with about ±0.1 of slack given the timing noise. Drag and wind also feed into drop 4's fall time, so the fit is only approximate, but it looks reasonable overall. Next I want to look at drop 4's residual in the vertical direction.

I'm checking whether the drop 4 residual, around +2, points to a consistent northward bias in the prediction. Wind direction 89 would need to shift south to correct that, but the earlier trial at 92 pushed drop 2 too far the other way, so the fix isn't obvious. Drag could also explain the pattern, so I'll look at fitting drag and the other parameters together.

I'm now looking at how the veer might show up across altitudes: my test drops span 40 to 150, and the wind direction estimates seem to shift with height. I'm starting a rough least-squares fit of direction against altitude to see whether that trend is real.

I'm working out the veer slope from the four direction estimates, which comes to about -1.2° per 100 m. The noise on that slope is roughly 5° per 100 m, so the veer could plausibly sit anywhere in about ±10°.

I'm weighing whether a veer of up to 10° per 100 m would matter, since at 40 m versus 100 m that could shift the impact by roughly 2 m. Shear and veer both affect the impact, so I'm considering whether more test drops are worth it, with six left, and whether to match the target's altitude and heading.

I'm now planning test drops at high and low altitudes, since the wind sample at each altitude is noisy and the spread across heights should show how the wind changes with height.

I'm planning the next test drops at 150 m and 30 m to pin down how the wind changes with height, starting with a drop at 150 m from a point about 350 m from the origin.

I'm settling on two more test drops, one at 30 m altitude heading 270 at speed 70, starting from about 354 m out, and running them alongside each other.

I'm pulling together the wind readings at each height: about 8.1 m/s at 150 m, 6.8 at 100 m, 5.2 at 40 m, and 5.7 at 30 m, with roughly 0.5 of noise. Next I'm starting to fit a wind shear exponent from the ratio between the 150 m and 100 m speeds.

Checking the shear exponent against the 40 m and 30 m readings gives lower values, around 0.27 and 0.15. The low-altitude points pull the estimate down, so I'm settling on a compromise near 0.35 and moving on to compare it against the six drops at my current best settings.

I'm seeing the residuals show y consistently overpredicted by about a meter and x mostly underpredicted on the far drops, with drop 5 at dx -2.5 and dy +1.9. I want to test veer and direction adjustments to correct that systematic offset.

I'm weighing a small wind-direction change against a modest speed increase to close the north and east residuals, since a shift past 90 degrees would only need about 0.8 degrees to cut the northward drift by a meter. I'll try a wind speed of 7.3 with a direction of 91 degrees.

Now I'm checking the dx residuals, which average around 1, against the earlier range that averaged -1.0. That makes a wind speed of 7.15 look roughly ideal, and a direction of 90 possibly right. The dy residuals average about -0.35, down from +1.2, and I'm wondering whether the shift from 89 to 91 degrees caused that change.

I'm trying a wind speed of 7.15 with direction 90, since the average dy shift implies the direction should sit near that value. I'm also noting that dropping the point with dx at 3.2 may matter, because its effect depends on the updraft, so I'll test it.

The residuals look about right at roughly a meter, which fits the noise level of 1.5, so the drop 4 and drop 3 offsets are probably just noise. Drop 4 was the smoke drop, and I'm wondering whether the updraft affects the horizontal drift through a change in fall time. Next I want to test veer by comparing the residuals at +10 and -10, and check shear too.

I'm checking the shear values next, around 0.25 and 0.45, though the data may not be sensitive to them. I'll start with veer by testing +10 first.

Veer at zero gives the lowest mean miss, while ±10 is clearly worse, so the best range looks like somewhere close to zero. Next I'll try shear values of 0.25 and 0.45 to see how sensitive the result is.

I've settled on a shear of 0.35, since it fits best compared with 0.25 and 0.45, and I'm considering that a range of about 0.35 to 0.38. I still want to check how wind speed and shear might vary together, and the updraft value is only inferred from targets with intensities between 0.5 and 1.4.

I'm weighing the remaining four test drops against refining the updraft estimate, since the target updraft scales with intensity and could reach about 5.3 m/s. Passing a drop through the smoke column would shift fall time and therefore drift, so a well-placed high-altitude release looks like the most sensitive way to pin down that value.

I'm working out where to release the test drop so the load stays in the updraft column longer, since a high, slow-moving drop from the center should let the updraft act for several seconds. The updraft strength itself is only roughly pinned down at about 3.8 m/s, and a residual of around 0.1 m/s seems good enough for the targets.

I'm thinking about whether a few more test drops would help, since wind speed and direction have the biggest effect on impact, and the current error is probably around half a meter.

I'll run two more high-speed drops at different headings from 150 and 120 m to tighten the wind estimate, since they cost nothing beyond the drop itself.

The residuals look within noise, so I'm settling on drag 0.0375, wind speed 7.15, direction 90, shear 0.35, veer 0, and updraft 3.8. I'll skip rechecking direction 89.5, since it isn't needed. With two test drops left unused, I'm moving on to start the operation and let the targets show positions and constraints.

The targets are over a kilometre away, and since the wind is uniform the drop has to be computed rather than eyeballed. Each fire has a smoke column with an updraft of roughly 2.7 to 4.1 m/s at peak, which I need to account for. For each target I'm working out the heading, altitude, speed, and release point that put the impact right on the fire centre, and I'll run the simulation with that target's updraft included.

I'm working out how to make the simulator's calibration fire at (0,0) stand in for each target. Since it only models that one fire, I'll shift the release point by the predicted displacement so the impact lands on the target, and check whether the smoke near the target changes the path.

I'm checking whether the smoke near the target bends the drop. My plan is to get the wind-only displacement from the simulator with the updraft set to zero, then estimate the extra fall time the smoke adds where the load passes through the column near the impact point.

Still checking how the target's smoke changes the load's fall time, since a few seconds in the column could shift the impact by around 9 m.

I'm checking whether translating the simulation by the target's offset gives an equivalent result, since the wind is uniform. The main mismatch is intensity: the simulator only models a fire with radius 50 m and updraft at intensity 1, so I'd need to match the target's updraft and accept a small radius difference.

I'm weighing whether the target's smoke can be avoided, since any drop aimed at the fire centre has to pass through the column near the ground, where the updraft is reduced but not zero.

I'm settling on how to pick each target's release point, including the smoke's updraft in the calculation. The column reaches down to the ground, so any drop landing at a fire's centre passes through it, and the simulator's updraft setting needs to be matched closely enough to account for that.

Picking mid-range values for the first target: heading 84, altitude 55, with the speed and release point to be worked out with the simulator.

I'm weighing a way to offset the release point so the simulator's fire at the origin matches the target's location, since the wind is uniform and the calculation should translate. The smoke effect breaks that exact equivalence, so I'm checking how the displacement changes with the release offset relative to the fire.

I'm treating the target's smoke as a shift in the frame: if the simulator's fire sits at the origin, I can move the release point by the target offset and iterate until the predicted impact lands on the fire centre. I'll start with the release at the origin to get the baseline displacement, then correct the offset from there.

I'm checking that the smoke shifts the impact point by only about 3 m at this altitude, so it's a minor effect. Working back from the displacement of about (89, 7), I'm estimating the release point needed to land near the origin, then planning to rerun the simulation from there with the updraft included to see how the smoke changes the result.

I'm checking the aircraft's heading from the release point, which works out to (1030, -300), with the plane flying heading 84 from there. Next I'll run the simulation at the offset Q = (-89, -7) to verify the result.

I'm setting the first target's drop point at (1030, -300) with heading 84, altitude 55, and speed 67, and I'm accepting the remaining uncertainty about the updraft peak and radius as good enough. For the second target, I'm weighing a heading range of 229 to 249 with altitude 110 to 130 and speed 50 to 60, and leaning toward heading 239, altitude 120, and speed 55.

I'm noting that the headings for target two point southwest, and I'll run the simulation with release at the origin.
I'm estimating D0 at roughly (11.7, -28.9), with the smoke-at-origin effect being small, so Q becomes (-11.7, 28.9). Next I want to check the simulation at Q.

I'm working out the second target's position by offsetting from the base coordinates, landing at about (-1161.7, 777.9). For the third target, I'm settling on heading 280, altitude 101, and speed 60, within the ranges I'd considered, with an updraft of 2.85.

I'm trying a release at Q=(8.5, -10.1), which gives an impact of (1.8, 0). To cancel that, I'll shift the release point to (6.7, -10.1), since impact roughly tracks Q plus a fixed offset D = (-6.7, 10.1). Working that through, the new release point should bring the impact to about (0, 0).

I'm settling on the release point at Q=(6.7, -10.1), treating the offset as roughly constant. Next I'm working out the target for stop 3, which lands at (217.7, -1511.1). Then I'm moving to target 4, picking heading 27, altitude 116 and speed 65 within the allowed ranges.
I'm correcting the point Q at (-82, -59.2) by the residual (1.9, -0.8), which gives (-83.9, -58.4). I'll double-check that arithmetic.

I'm working out Target 4's position by subtracting the offsets from its coordinates, landing at about (-1518.9, -1222.4). Target 5 is next: I'm reading its bounds for heading, altitude, and speed, then settling on heading 105, altitude 77, and speed 55, with an updraft of 3.34.

I'm settling on the corrected point at (-93.2, 16.1), which puts P5 at (873.8, 1229.1). The residual is small, so I'm going with that value. Next I'll weigh how sensitive the result is to the updraft estimate and its uncertainty, since the targets sit roughly 1100 to 1500 m out and the 6 m drop error seems tolerable. I'm also starting to check the constraints against their ranges.

I'm checking each target's heading, altitude, and speed against its allowed range, and they all fall within bounds. Then I'm dropping the payload.
